questionStem: A 6-hour-old female newborn has had cyanosis of her arms and legs since birth. She was born at 38 weeks' gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy and cesarean delivery for breech presentation . She weighed 3090 g (6 lb 13 oz) at birth. She has been breast-feeding well. She is alert and is not in acute distress . Her rectal temperature is 36.2°C (97.2°F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 36/min , and blood pressure is 80/45 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. Examination shows cyanosis of the upper and lower extremities but no circumoral cyanosis . Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities . Capillary refill time is mildly delayed . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Placement of the newborn under warming lights

correctExplanation: This neonate has a slightly decreased body temperature of 36.2°C (97.2°F) while her other vital signs are within normal limits for a neonate. Cyanosis of the extremities and delayed capillary refill time are manifestations of mild hypothermia. Neonates, particularly preterm neonates, have a high body surface area relative to their mass which makes them prone to rapid heat loss and the development of hypothermia. Neonatal hypothermia requires prompt correction as it is associated with increased mortality. Hypothermia increases oxygen consumption and metabolic demands on the neonate which leads to less successful resuscitation efforts if they are needed. Interventions directed at temperature regulation immediately after delivery include increasing the temperature of the delivery room, placing the neonate in skin-to-skin contact with its mother immediately after birth, using a radiant heater during resuscitation, and swaddling after drying.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hypothermia can be a sign of systemic illness, such as sepsis, but in this neonate with relatively mild hypothermia and an otherwise normal course in the first 6 hours after delivery, systemic illness is unlikely. Blood culture (Choice B) is unnecessary. This infant is mildly cyanotic in the extremities because of the vasoconstrictive response to the cold environment, not as a result of respiratory distress or a congenital heart defect. Respirations of 36/min and an oxygen saturation of 96% are within normal limits, and cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Thus, neither a chest x-ray (Choice C) nor intubation and mechanical ventilation (Choice E) are needed at this time. Likewise, there is nothing to suggest a congenital heart defect as the cause of her cyanosis, so an echocardiography (Choice D) is not needed at this time. Educational Objective: Neonatal hypothermia may develop after delivery as a result of rapid heat loss of the neonate. Cyanosis of the extremities and delayed capillary refill time are manifestations of such. Neonatal hypothermia requires prompt correction as it is associated with increased mortality. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 2-year-old girl is brought for a follow-up examination 2 days after initiating amoxicillin therapy for a right lower lobe pneumonia . She had been healthy prior to onset of the pneumonia . She continues to have fevers and cough , and she now has right-sided chest pain. Her immunizations are up-to-date . She appears ill and is tachypneic . Her temperature is 38.5°C (101 .3°F), pulse is 140/min, and respirations are 45/min . Repeat x-rays of the chest show a large dense consolidation in the right lower lung field and a fixed right-sided effusion . Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
correctExplanation: Pneumonia in patients under the age of 5 is a common cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Causative organisms in the pediatric population depend on the age of the patient. In the neonatal period, patients are at risk for infection from microbes present in the vaginal canal including Streptococcus agalactiae (group B), Klebsiella, Escherichia coli, and Listeria monocytogenes. In patients between the ages of 2 and 5 years, viral pneumonia is most common. Bacterial pathogens include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Staphylococcus aureus. The risk for H. influenzae type b infection is reduced in patients with up-to-date immunizations. Staphylococcus aureus commonly expresses beta-lactamases, which confer resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics such as amoxicillin, and combination therapy with a beta-lactam or a beta-lactamase inhibitor (eg, amoxicillin-clavulanic acid) is recommended. Pneumonia may be complicated by a parapneumonic effusion, which should be evaluated by thoracentesis.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Enterobacter cloacae (Choice A) is a Gram-negative, facultative anaerobe that makes up normal gut flora. It is associated with skin and soft tissue, urinary tract, and respiratory infections, especially in immunocompromised patients. It would be an unusual cause of pneumonia in this otherwise healthy patient. Haemophi/us influenzae type b (Choice B) is an encapsulated, Gram-negative coccobacillus and a common cause of pneumonia in the pediatric and adult populations. Areas with widespread childhood immunization have significantly lower risk for contracting H. influenzae pneumonia. Mycobacterium avium-intracel/ulare (Choice C) is a non-tuberculosis acid-fast bacillus that may cause pneumonia when organisms are inhaled from the environment. Severe and disseminated disease can occur in immunocompromised patients. Staphylococcus aureus is a more common cause of pneumonia. Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Choice D) is a Gram-negative bacillus ubiquitous in the environment. It can result in numerous clinical infectious conditions, including urinary tract infections, osteomyelitis, otitis externa, folliculitis, hospital or ventilator-associated pneumonia, and sepsis. Pseudomonas pneumonia is associated with cystic fibrosis. Educational Objective: Pneumonia is common in the pediatric population, and is typically caused by respiratory viruses, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Staphylococcus aureus. Immunization programs against Haemophilus influenzae type b have reduced the prevalence of this disease. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 16-year-old boy who plays soccer has the acute onset of fever, malaise , and pain in his left lower extremity. He is unable to walk. He appears ill. His temperature is 39.4 °C (103°F). He has limited movement of the lower extremity and swelling and point tenderness over the proximal medial lower leg. There is no overlying contusion or break in the skin. His hemoglobin concentration is 12 g/dl , leukocyte count is 14,000/mm 3, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 60 mm/h. A technetium 99m bone scan shows uptake at the metaphysis of the tibia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Osteomyelitis is an infection of bone and bone marrow, and typically presents acutely, subacutely, or chronically from direct inoculation or hematogenous spread from a distal site. Acute osteomyelitis is more common in children and is most often caused by infection with Staphylococcus aureus. Risk factors include traumatic inoculating injury, diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, intravenous substance use, and prosthetic devices or indwelling hardware. Patients typically complain of pain, difficulty bearing weight, and overlying erythema. Laboratory studies may show leukocytosis and increased inflammatory markers. Imaging typically shows localized osseous erosive changes. Bone scintigraphy with the radiotracer technetium 99m may show increased uptake in the area of infection.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Osgood-Schlatter disease (Choice B) refers to osteochondrosis or traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle that typically occurs in adolescent, athletic children . This presents with progressive pain along the anterior aspect of the proximal tibia and knee that is exacerbated by kneeling. Physical examination typically discloses tenderness over an enlarged tibial tubercle. Patients do not present with inability to bear weight or fever. Fracture of the tibia (Choice C) presents with acute pain, inability to bear weight on the extremity, and localized edema and tenderness in the area of injury. Fever, leukocytosis, and increased inflammatory markers would be unusual. Bone scintigraphy may be useful for detecting occult fractures, but x-ray or CT scan would be the initial modality of choice. Prepatellar bursitis (Choice D) refers to inflammation of the bursa overlying the patella. Common causes include infection, trauma, and recurrent pressure (as from occupations that require frequent kneeling). A bone scan would show no abnormalities. Septic arthritis (Choice E) results from bacterial infection of the synovial joint space, most commonly by S. aureus. The affected joint demonstrates pain, swelling, and erythema. Arthrocentesis is indicated for the evaluation of monoarticular erythema and swelling to evaluate for septic arthritis, which characteristically shows purulent synovial fluid with >50,000 WBC/mm 3• Physical examination would disclose a tender, erythematous, and edematous joint, which is not present in this case. Educational Objective: Osteomyelitis is an infection of the bone or bone marrow that may be caused by direct local spread of an infection or hematogenous seeding from a distal site. Patients present with fever, localized pain and inflammation, and increased inflammatory markers. Imaging may show inflammatory and destructive bony changes. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 6-day-old girl is brought to the physician because of vomiting for 2 days . She has not had fever. She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy , labor, and delivery. Results of newborn screening are pending . She was discharged at the age of 1 day. She is exclusively breast-fed and is feeding every 3 hours. She is at the 50th percentile for length and head circumference and 5th percentile for weight. Examination shows generalized jaundice . The liver is enlarged and firm. Her serum total bilirubin concentration is 14 mg/dL , with a direct component of 8 mg/dl. Test of the urine for reducing substances is positive . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis ?
correctExplanation: Galactosemia is the most likely diagnosis in this exclusively breast-fed patient with hepatomegaly and the presence of reducing substances in the urine. Normal metabolism of lactose involves separation into glucose and galactose by lactase. Free glucose can be used for cellular energy production while galactose must be converted to galactose-1-phosphate by galactokinase and then subsequently converted to UDP-galactose and then glucose-1-phosphate by galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT). While galactosemia can result from deficiencies in several different enzymes in this pathway, deficiency of GALT causes classic galactosemia, which is an autosomal recessive disorder. Breast milk contains galactose, which patients with galactosemia are unable to break down. Early complications include jaundice, vomiting, hepatomegaly, diarrhea, lethargy, and occasionally sepsis with Gram-negative organisms. Coagulopathy and easy bruising may also occur. Diagnosis is made by assessing for the presence and activity of GALT in erythrocytes by radioimmunoassay. Reducing substances are molecules that can convert cupric to cuprous ions in the urine and include glucose, lactose, pentose, and galactose. The presence of these substances (galactose) can suggest the diagnosis but is not specific. Additionally, while galactosemia is detected on newborn screening, manifestations of the disease can occur before the results of screening are available. Treatment requires eliminating dietary galactose and providing necessary supplements, however, this may not reverse neurologic sequelae of the disease, such as infantile cataracts and intellectual disability.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hereditary fructose intolerance (Choice B) is caused by a deficiency in aldolase B, an enzyme important in the metabolism of fructose. Deficiency results in increased concentrations offructose-1-phosphate and fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, causing a deficiency of available phosphate, which inhibits gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. Patients present with hypoglycemia only after fructose is introduced into the diet. Mucopolysaccharidosis II (Choice C), also known as Hunter syndrome, is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a deficiency in iduronate-2-sulfatase, which results in the deposition of heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate. Within the first year of life, patients develop coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, hernias, and dysostosis multiplex. Type I glycogen storage disease (Choice D) is caused by glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency. This enzyme is located in the liver and functions in gluconeogenesis to convert glucose-6-phosphate to glucose for its release into the blood. Impaired gluconeogenesis can lead to severe hypoglycemia during periods of fasting. It is characterized by excess glycogen in the liver, hepatomegaly, and fasting hypoglycemia. Tyrosinemia (Choice E) can refer to one of several disorders in which enzymes required for the metabolism of tyrosine are deficient. In its most severe form, it can present with liver disease and renal tubular acidosis, but hypophosphatemia, bone mineralization disorders, and aminoaciduria are also potential findings. Educational Objective: Galactosemia refers to defects in enzymes that metabolize galactose. Classic galactosemia results from the deficiency of GALT, which converts galactose-1-phosphate to UDP-galactose and then glucose-1-phosphate. Early manifestations include jaundice, hepatomegaly, hypotonia, and sepsis. Reducing substances in the urine are often present but not specific. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 2-hour-old newborn has a large fluctuant area of swelling in the left parietal region. She was born at term following a difficult forceps delivery. The newborn is alert and in no distress . Examination of the area shows margins limited by suture lines. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the swelling?

choices.B: Blood under the periosteum of the parietal bone
choices.C: Cerebrospinal fluid under the galea aponeurotica
choices.D: Cerebrospinal fluid under the periosteum of the parietal bone

correctExplanation: Cephalohematomas are traumatic subperiosteal hematomas that can occur with uncomplicated or assisted vaginal deliveries. They present as cranial swelling that does not cross suture lines. This is in contrast to caput succedaneum, which is a supra-periosteal hematoma that does cross suture lines. Most commonly, cephalohematomas self-resolve without intervention. Complications include calcification of the hematoma with prolonged bony swelling and cranial deformities, infection, and osteomyelitis. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia can occur because of the resorption of extravasated blood products.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Blood under the galea aponeurotica (Choice A) describes a subgaleal hemorrhage, which occurs secondary to trauma sustained during vaginal or assisted vaginal deliveries. It occurs because of shearing of the emissary veins that connect the scalp to the dural sinuses, and it carries the potential for significant hemorrhage. It presents with a diffuse swelling of the head that continues to worsen after delivery, tachycardia, and pallor. Cerebrospinal fluid under the galea aponeurotica (Choice C) and under the periosteum of the parietal bone (Choice D) could occur following skull fractures, which are rare complications of uncomplicated and assisted vaginal deliveries. These can present with leptomeningeal cysts. Contusion of the scalp (Choice E) is commonly to the result of injury to the head, which causes damage to small blood vessels. It would present as ecchymosis, rather than a fluctuant swelling over the parietal area. Educational Objective: Cephalohematomas are traumatic subperiosteal hematomas that can occur as complications of uncomplicated or assisted vaginal deliveries. They result in fluctuant swelling that does not cross suture lines. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 3-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the onset of lethargy. There is no history of trauma , and she has not had fever, diarrhea , or vomiting . She was born at 27 weeks' gestation , and required 2 months of ventilatory support and a 2-week course of dexamethasone therapy for respiratory distress syndrome of the newborn and bronchopulmonary dysplasia . She had an umbilical arterial and venous catheter in place during the first 2 weeks of life. Her temperature is 36. 7°C (98.1 °F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 20/min , and blood pressure is 110/85 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation . Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities . Doppler ultrasonography shows renal artery thrombosis . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's hypertension?
correctExplanation: Renal artery thrombosis is a rare complication of umbilical artery catheterization that can present up to several weeks after the catheter has been removed. Other risk factors include sepsis, volume depletion, and a patent ductus arteriosus. Occlusion of the renal artery by the thrombus results in decreased afferent blood flow to the affected kidney and increased renin production from the juxtaglomerular apparatus. The overstimulation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system results in secondary hypertension. Treatment of renal artery thrombosis includes systemic anticoagulation and volume resuscitation. Unilateral nephrectomy may be required in refractory hypertension.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (Choice A) can result in pulmonary hypertension as a result of chronic hypoxia and vascular remodeling, which commonly occurs in adults. It would be unlikely in a 3-month-old patient. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (Choice B), also called pseudotumor cerebri, is a condition of increased intracranial pressure without an identifiable cause. It most commonly presents in younger female patients; risk factors include obesity, and use of vitamin A, oral contraceptives, or danazol. It is usually associated with a holocephalic headache and blurry vision. Prematurity (Choice D) is a risk factor for surfactant deficiency and neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Steroid therapy is indicated to promote surfactant production. Prolonged use of corticosteroids (Choice E) can result in hypertension as a result of the increased fluid retention from mineralocorticoid effects on the kidneys. Dexamethasone is a potent glucocorticoid that has minimal mineralocorticoid effects and is unlikely to produce significant hypertension, especially weeks after exposure. Educational Objective: Impaired perfusion to one or both of the kidneys is a potential cause of secondary hypertension. Renal artery thrombosis is a rare disorder associated with umbilical artery catheterization. Occlusion of the renal artery by the thrombus results in decreased afferent blood flow to the affected kidney and increased renin production from the juxtaglomerular apparatus. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 3-month-old infant is inactive and slow in feeding and has constipation . Her serum thyroxine (T 4) concentration is decreased and serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration is increased . Which of the following is the most likely cause?
correctExplanation: Thyroid dysgenesis involves the underdevelopment or complete absence of thyroid tissue. It is commonly caused by a mutation in PAXB, encoding a paired box transcription factor. Paired box transcription factors are crucial for the proper embryologic development of tissues throughout the body, and mutations in paired box genes cause a variety of diseases characterized by improper tissue development, such as Waardenburg syndrome, aniridia, ocular coloboma, optic nerve hypoplasia, oligodontia, and kidney hypoplasia. Thyroid dysgenesis presents in infancy with symptoms of hypothyroidism, such as lethargy, poor feeding, and constipation. Characteristically, serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentrations are increased, and serum concentrations of thyroid hormone are decreased or absent.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Deficiency in T 4-binding globulin (Choice A) is a rare, inherited condition that is usually asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on thyroid laboratory studies. It is not a common cause of symptomatic hypothyroidism. Hypopituitarism (Choice B) may cause secondary hypothyroidism because of the inadequate production of TSH. TSH concentrations would be decreased, which is not consistent with this patient's laboratory findings. Lymphocytic thyroiditis (Choice C), also known as Hashimoto disease, is the most common form of thyroiditis and presents with signs and symptoms of hypothyroidism. Hashimoto disease most commonly affects middle aged women, although teens and rarely children can be affected. During infancy, Hashimoto disease is rare, and alternate diagnoses such as thyroid dysgenesis are more likely. Unresponsiveness to thyroid hormone (Choice E) is a rare disorder characterized by diffuse peripheral tissue unresponsiveness to binding of the thyroid hormone receptor by thyroid hormone. It may present with goiter and symptoms of hypothyroidism. Serum concentrations of T 4 are characteristically increased in order to overcome the unresponsiveness of the peripheral tissues. Educational Objective: Thyroid dysgenesis involves the underdevelopment or complete absence of thyroid tissue. Thyroid dysgenesis presents in infancy with symptoms of hypothyroidism, such as lethargy, poor feeding, and constipation. Characteristically, serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentrations are increased, and serum concentrations of thyroid hormone are decreased or absent. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 2-week-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents because of a 30-minute history of her chest "fluttering ." Thirty minutes ago, she vomited after breast-feeding . She was born at 40 weeks' gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. She weighed 3402 g (7 lb 8 oz) at birth. On arrival , she is awake and appears alert. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is too rapid to count , respirations are 48/min , and blood pressure is 74/48 mm Hg. The extremities are pink and warm ; capillary refill time is less than 2 seconds . The lungs are clear to auscultation . No murmurs are heard on cardiac examination . An ECG shows a regular heart rate of 240/min , a ORS complex duration of 0.05 seconds , and no discernible P waves . Application of an ice bag to the face for 5 seconds does not change the heart rate . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) commonly occurs in children and infants and is characterized by paroxysmal episodes of rapid, narrow-complex tachycardia. SVT is often idiopathic and paroxysmal but may occur secondary to accessory pathways in some children with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. Diagnosis is made by ECG, although some children may require cardiac monitoring in order to capture a paroxysmal event. AV nodal blockade with adenosine is the first line treatment for narrow complex SVT. Adenosine is a purine analogue that acts on the adenosine receptor, a G protein-coupled receptor that signals through adenylate cyclase. In the AV node, binding of the adenosine Arreceptor leads to cellular hyperpolarization and reduced transmission of supraventricular action potentials. If adenosine fails, synchronized cardioversion may be attempted. Children who are old enough may be trained to use vagal maneuvers in order to naturally induce AV nodal blockade. A similar vagal maneuver may be attempted by placing an ice bag over the eyes and face for approximately 30 seconds.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Administration of digoxin {Choice B) is useful in the management of congestive heart failure and of atrial fibrillation and flutter. It is not used in the treatment of SVT. Administration of procainamide {Choice C), a sodium channel blocker, may be useful in achieving chemical cardioversion in atrial fibrillation, but is not a first line agent for the treatment of SVT when narrow complex. It is commonly used in arrhythmia management in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, especially in cases of antidromic reentrant tachycardia. Administration of verapamil {Choice D), a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, is useful for control of SVT but is not a first-line agent for aborting the acute arrhythmia. It is also useful for the management of cluster headache. Catheter ablation {Choice E) is useful for the treatment of accessory pathways in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. While Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome may be diagnosed in infancy, paroxysmal SVT is more common. Unsynchronized cardioversion {Choice F) delivers an electrical shock at any point within the cardiac cycle. This method is reserved for pulseless ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation. In patients with SVT who fail treatment with adenosine, synchronized cardioversion is preferred. Educational Objective: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) commonly occurs in children and infants and is characterized by paroxysmal episodes of rapid, narrow-complex tachycardia. AV nodal blockade with adenosine is the first-line treatment. In the AV node, binding the adenosine Arreceptor leads to cellular hyperpolarization and reduced transmission of supraventricular action potentials. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: An otherwise asymptomatic 4-week-old boy is brought to the physician because of increasing jaundice for 1 week . He was born at term following a prolonged labor. One day after birth, he received phototherapy for jaundice and was discharged on the third day. He is exclusively breast-fed . Examination shows no abnormalities except for jaundice . Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 12 g/dl with normal red cell morphology , and a total serum bilirubin concentration of 12 mg/dl with a direct component of 8 mg/dl. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's jaundice ?

choices.C: Decreased hepatic Y and Z protein concentrations

correctExplanation: Neonatal jaundice with a preponderance of conjugated bilirubin, as indicated by an increased direct bilirubin, is suggestive of biliary atresia. Biliary atresia is caused by the abnormal underdevelopment of the extrahepatic biliary system. Affected infants are able to conjugate bilirubin normally in the liver but are unable to excrete bile into the gastrointestinal lumen. Affected infants present with worsening jaundice caused by conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, along with pale stool, dark urine, poor weight gain, and, in untreated cases, cirrhosis, coagulopathy, and portal hypertension. Conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and therefore does not cause kernicterus. Treatment includes surgical portoenterostomy to allow bile to be excreted or a liver transplant.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Decreased hepatic glucuronosyltransferase activity (Choice B) underlies the pathogenesis of Gilbert syndrome and Crigler-Najjar syndrome. Both of these diseases are characterized by defective hepatic conjugation of bilirubin. Accumulation of unconjugated bilirubin is identified by an increased serum concentration of indirect bilirubin. Decreased hepatic Y and Z protein concentrations (Choice C) would interfere with hepatic bilirubin conjugation. These two proteins are involved in the cytosolic binding of bilirubin in hepatocytes and allow for the transport of bilirubin to the smooth endoplasmic reticulum for metabolic processing. Decreased serum bilirubin uptake (Choice D) would occur in hypoalbuminemia. Circulating serum bilirubin is unconjugated and water insoluble. Normal transport of serum bilirubin to the liver is dependent upon normal concentrations of albumin, to which bilirubin is bound and thereby solubilized. Increased serum bilirubin production (Choice E) is suggestive of hemolytic disease, such as sickle cell disease. lntravascular hemolysis can be identified by increased serum concentrations of indirect, or unconjugated, bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase, and decreased serum concentrations of haptoglobin. Educational Objective: Biliary atresia is caused by the abnormal underdevelopment of the extrahepatic biliary system. Affected infants present with worsening jaundice caused by conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, along with pale stool, dark urine, poor weight gain, and, in untreated cases, cirrhosis, coagulopathy, and portal hypertension. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother for a well-child examination . She is at the 50th percentile for length and weight. A grade 2/6, crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur with a musical quality is heard best at the lower left sternal border with no radiation . S2 is normal. Precordial activity and peripheral pulses are normal. There were no previous notations of a murmur in her medical records . An ECG shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Reassurance that this is a benign murmu

correctExplanation: A Still murmur is a benign, asymptomatic murmur heard in children. It is a systolic, musical, grade 1 to 2 murmur best heard at the lower left sternal border. It is typically louder when the patient is supine than when the patient is sitting. It most commonly self-resolves by adolescence. Pathologic murmurs are more frequently heard in infants under one year of age, caused by abnormalities such as valve disorders or shunt lesions, whereas murmurs heard after one year of age are more frequently benign, although they can be caused by valve stenosis, regurgitation, or atrial septal defects. Pathologic murmurs also present with related symptoms, such as dyspnea, diaphoresis, or failure to thrive. Further evaluation is recommended for murmurs that are grade 3 or greater in intensity, diastolic, at maximal intensity at the left upper sternal border, holosystolic, or have a harsh or blowing quality. It is also recommended for murmurs that are more intense in the upright position. As this patient has a benign Still murmur, reassurance is appropriate.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Complete blood count (CBC) (Choice B) could be used to evaluate for infection or anemia as a cause of the murmur. Endocarditis causes lesions of the heart valves that can present with heart murmurs as well as leukocytosis on CBC, whereas severe anemia can lead to a functional murmur. This patient has a benign murmur; a CBC is not indicated. Chest x-rays (Choice C) can be used in the initial evaluation of cyanotic and non-cyanotic congenital heart disease. For example, tetralogy of Fallo! can present with a systolic ejection murmur heard in the left upper sternal border because of pulmonic stenosis, as well as a boot-shaped heart on chest x-ray. However, a chest x-ray in this patient would show no abnormalities. Echocardiography (Choice D) is used to evaluate the structure and function of the heart. If this patient had a concerning murmur, such as a diastolic grade 4/6 murmur, echocardiography would be the most appropriate next step. However, it plays no role in the evaluation of this benign murmur. Antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures (Choice E) is recommended to prevent the development of infective endocarditis for patients with prosthetic heart valves, unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, repaired congenital heart disease (with residual shunts, valvular regurgitation, or an occlusion device), or valve regurgitation in a transplanted heart. This patient does not require antibiotic prophylaxis. Educational Objective: A Still murmur is a benign, asymptomatic murmur of childhood that presents with a systolic, grade 1 to 2 murmur with a musical quality best heard at the lower left sternal border. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 17-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 40 minutes after being stabbed in the left side of her chest with a pair of scissors . En route to the hospital , intravenous lactated Ringer solution was administered , and administration of oxygen (3 Umin) via face mask was begun . On arrival, she has severe chest pain. She is agitated and diaphoretic and is not oriented to person , place, or time . Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 32/min and labored , and palpable systolic blood pressure is 80 mm Hg. Examination shows jugular venous distention bilaterally. The trachea is deviated to the right. Breath sounds are decreased on the left with hyperresonance to percussion . Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
correctExplanation: Tension pneumothorax can be a complication of a penetrating thoracic trauma and occurs when air is able to enter the pleural space but is prevented from exiting. Increasing amounts of trapped air in the pleural space compresses the lung parenchyma, creating an inability for the lung to expand and causing it to collapse. As the pneumothorax progresses and continues to increase in size, it can result in tracheal or mediastinal deviation away from the affected hemithorax. It can also result in compression of the pulmonary veins and superior vena cava, decreasing venous return to the left and right atria, which manifests with hypotension, jugular venous distension, and obstructive shock. Tension pneumothorax is characterized by absent breath sounds and hyperresonance to percussion caused by increased air in the intrathoracic space displacing normal lung parenchyma. In an unstable patient, air from a tension pneumothorax should be evacuated by an emergent needle decompression followed by a tube thoracostomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Chest x-ray (Choice A) would not be the appropriate next step in management of this unstable patient. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, and immediate management should involve evacuation of air from the intrapleural space. Insertion of an oropharyngeal airway (Choice B) is indicated during bag-valve mask ventilation of a patient, especially in cases of a tongue obstructing the airway. It is an adjunct that helps open the airway to allow for easier ventilation. Pericardiocentesis (Choice D) is appropriate in cases of pericardia! effusion or tamponade, which typically present following symptoms of pericarditis, or with muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distention, and hypotension if tamponade from any cause is present. Pulsus paradoxus may be disclosed on examination. This patient's jugular venous distension is a result of tension pneumothorax, not pericardia! tamponade. Cricothyroidotomy (Choice E) is a type of invasive airway access. It may be indicated in cases of airway compromise in which endotracheal intubation is unsuccessful. Educational Objective: Tension pneumothorax occurs when air is able to enter the pleural space but is prevented from exiting. This leads to an increasing amount of air trapped in the pleural space with subsequent collapse of the lung parenchyma and mass effect on the mediastinum. It is characterized by respiratory distress, tracheal deviation, hypotension, decreased breath sounds, and hyperresonance to percussion on physical examination. Management requires emergent needle decompression followed by placement of a chest tube. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by police because of a 5-hour history of hallucinations , profuse sweating , and intermittent yelling and flailing . He is striking out at those near him and requires leather restraints . His pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min , and blood pressure is 150/85 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pallor, profuse diaphoresis , and recent bruising . Mental status examination shows incoherent speech , episodic screaming, and agitation . He is disoriented to person , place, and time . The most appropriate next step in management is administration of which of the following?
correctExplanation: Phencyclidine (PCP) is an illicit substance that acts on the central nervous system in a variety of ways. It antagonizes NMDA receptors leading to excitatory neurotransmitter release, inhibits reuptake of dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, and stimulates alpha-adrenergic receptors. Acute PCP intoxication can lead to psychosis, bizarre behavior, agitation, aggression, rotatory nystagmus, and ataxia. Patients may be diaphoretic, tachycardic, and hypertensive because of sympathomimetic effects. Chronic PCP use can lead to major depressive disorder, psychotic symptoms, memory loss, and dysarthria. Control of psychomotor agitation is the first step in management of patients with PCP intoxication for the safety of the patient and medical staff. Chemical sedation with benzodiazepines such as intramuscular lorazepam or midazolam can be administered to control symptoms. Once a patient is adequately sedated, further evaluation can be completed to assess for traumatic injuries or complications of PCP intoxication such as rhabdomyolysis, hyperthermia, hypertension, seizures, encephalopathy, or a comatose state.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Intramuscular naloxone (Choice B) is indicated for cases of opioid overdose. Opioid overdoses are characterized by respiratory depression presenting as a decreased respiratory rate, apnea, and hypoxia. This patient is severely agitated, making PCP intoxication more likely. Intravenous 50% dextrose (Choice C) is indicated in hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemia can cause confusion, altered mental status, lightheadedness, and syncope. Hypoglycemia would be unlikely to cause hypertension and psychomotor agitation as seen in this patient. Intravenous flumazenil (Choice D) is indicated for benzodiazepine overdose. It is a competitive inhibitor of the GABA receptor at the benzodiazepine binding site. Benzodiazepine overdose is characterized by sedation and potential respiratory depression, not psychomotor agitation as seen in this patient. Intravenous 5% glucose and 0.9% saline (Choice E) are typically administered as maintenance fluids in patients who are unable to tolerate oral nutrition or for patients who are fasting prior to a surgical procedure. It would not help in sedating this patient. Educational Objective: Acute PCP intoxication can lead to psychosis, bizarre behavior, agitation, aggression, rotatory nystagmus, and ataxia. Control of psychomotor agitation is the first step in management of patients with PCP intoxication for the safety of the patient and medical staff. Chemical sedation with benzodiazepines such as intramuscular lorazepam or midazolam can be administered to control symptoms. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of lower abdominal cramps and intermittent pain in her knees and hips for 6 weeks . The cramps are relieved by bowel movements . During this period , she has had 6 to 10 urgent, bloody bowel movements daily. Examination shows a swollen , mildly tender left knee joint. Her hemoglobin concentration is 14.5 g/dl , leukocyte count is 16,000/mm 3, and platelet count is 790,000/mm 3. Analysis of knee joint aspirate shows straw-colored , slightly turbid fluid with a leukocyte count of 2000/mm 3 (40% segmented neutrophils) . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Ulcerative colitis is a type of inflammatory bowel disease that results in inflammation and ulceration of the colonic mucosa and submucosa, typically beginning in the rectum and advancing proximally in a continuous distribution. Symptoms include chronic abdominal pain, weight loss, bloody diarrhea, abdominal bloating, and tenesmus. Imaging typically demonstrates loss of haustral markings. Diagnosis of ulcerative colitis is by colonoscopy and biopsy, which demonstrates characteristic crypt abscesses. Potential complications of ulcerative colitis are fulminant colitis, toxic megacolon, and perforation. Inflammatory bowel disease can also be associated with extraintestinal manifestations including uveitis, arthritis, aphthous stomatitis, and pyoderma gangrenosum. Treatment includes immunomodulators, biologics, and steroids, although total colectomy is generally curative and would eliminate the patient's risk for colorectal carcinoma.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adenovirus gastroenteritis (Choice A) is a cause of self-limited viral gastroenteritis with acute nausea, vomiting, and non-bloody diarrhea. It would be unlikely to cause bloody diarrhea and 6 weeks of symptoms. Chronic nonspecific diarrhea of childhood (Choice B) is an idiopathic condition characterized by diarrhea in otherwise healthy children. It does not cause weight loss, abdominal pain, or bloody stools. Giardiasis (Choice C) presents with foul-smelling, fatty diarrhea, and bloating, typically in campers who ingest cysts from freshwater. It does not typically cause bloody stools. Henoch-Schonlein purpura (Choice D) is a small-vessel vasculitis that occurs in children and typically presents with gravity-dependent purpura (eg, buttocks, legs, and feet), arthralgias, hematuria, and abdominal pain (eg, intussusception). Pseudomembranous colitis (Choice E) is caused by C/ostridium difficile, which produces toxins that result in dysfunction of the brush border and a subsequent secretory diarrhea. C. difficile infections are associated with the presence of pseudomembranes that appear as patchy regions of white mucosa on colonoscopy. C. difficile infection is an opportunistic and often hospital-acquired infection that commonly occurs after the use of antibiotics, especially ampicillin and clindamycin, as a result of the loss of native colonic microbiota. Educational Objective: Ulcerative colitis is an inflammatory bowel disease that results in inflammation and ulceration of the colonic mucosa and submucosa. Symptoms include chronic abdominal pain, weight loss, bloody diarrhea, abdominal bloating, and tenesmus. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of right scrotal pain and swelling for 3 hours. There is no history of trauma . He was sexually active 3 months ago , and he did not use a condom . Examination shows tenderness and edema in the region of the right testicle . The cremasteric reflex is absent on the right side. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?

choices.C: Persistent patency of the processus vaginal is

correctExplanation: Testicular torsion occurs when the testicle rotates about itself within the scrotal sac. The resultant twisting of the spermatic cord, which contains the gonadal artery, pampiniform plexus, and gonadal vein, results in vascular congestion and potential cessation of venous or arterial flow to the testis. Patients typically present with acute, severe testicular pain with diffuse tenderness and swelling. Patients may also exhibit nausea, vomiting, and lower abdominal pain. There is typically a negative cremasteric reflex with a high-riding, transverse lie of the testicle on physical examination. If not properly and expeditiously managed with surgical detorsion and orchiopexy, testicular torsion can result in testicular infarction as well as infertility.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Leukemic infiltration of the testis (Choice A) is seen in acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Because of the blood-testis barrier, chemotherapy is less able to reach the testis. Testicular leukemia presents as painless testicular enlargement. Malignant infiltration of the testis (Choice B) can occur in testicular tumors such as seminoma, choriocarcinoma, teratoma, embryonal carcinoma, or yolk sac tumor. Presentation is variable depending on the type of tumor. Seminoma is the most common testicular tumor and presents as painless testicular enlargement. Persistent patency of the processus vaginalis (Choice C) can lead to the formation of a hydrocele if filled by peritoneal fluid, or hematocele if complicated by blood accumulation. It also increases the risk for an indirect inguinal hernia. Persistent patency of the urachus (Choice D) contributes to a persistent connection between the bladder and the umbilicus. Patients with a patent urachus can present with clear urine leaking out of the umbilicus. It can also be asymptomatic or potentially complicated by infection. Educational Objective: Testicular torsion occurs when the testicle rotates about itself within the scrotal sac. The resultant twisting of the spermatic cord, which contains the gonadal artery, pampiniform plexus, and gonadal vein, results in vascular congestion and potential cessation of venous or arterial flow. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A healthy 9-month-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents for a well-child examination . Her parents are concerned that she is not gaining enough weight. She is breast-feeding six times daily and taking small amounts of baby food from a spoon. She is at the 5th percentile for weight and 25th percentile for length and head circumference . Review of the growth chart shows that this growth pattern has been consistent since birth. Physical examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Reassurance that this growth i:>attern is within normal limits
choices.B: Increasing caloric intake by adding more baby food
choices.D: Supplementing breast-feeding with whole cow milk

correctExplanation: Growth charts show the percentile curves of body measurements such as head circumference, body weight, and length for children. They are used to evaluate for normal growth, short stature, growth delay, failure to thrive, nutritional deficiencies, malabsorption, endocrinopathy, and other disorders. Clinicians use the growth chart provided by the World Health Organization (WHO), which is an international standard for infant growth. For infants less than 2 years of age, infants are classified as low weight or short stature if they are less than 2nd percentile for weight or length, respectively. This patient is the 5th percentile for weight, which, while low, is not yet of concern. In addition, her growth pattern has been consistent since birth. Further assessment to investigate growth or nutritional problems should be performed if infants are less than the 2nd percentile or if there are major changes in growth pattern.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Increasing caloric intake by adding more baby food (Choice B) would not be an appropriate recommendation, as the patient's weight and length are within normal limits on the growth chart. This may be an appropriate recommendation if the patient's weight was less than the 2nd percentile and the reason for growth delay was inadequate caloric intake. Replacing breast-feeding with soy-based formula (Choice C) would not be appropriate. Breastfeeding is a standard source of nutrition for the growth and healthy development of infants. Supplementing breast-feeding with whole cow milk (Choice D) would be harmful to the infant. Early introduction of whole cow's milk prior to one year of age has been associated with type 1 diabetes mellitus, increased risk for developing cow's milk allergy, constipation, and iron deficiency anemia. Educational Objective: Growth charts show the percentile curves of body measurements such as head circumference, body weight, and length for children. Patients less than 2 years of age are classified as low weight or short stature if they are less than the 2nd percentile for weight or length, respectively. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: An otherwise healthy 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of a 6-month history of increasingly severe pain with menses . Her mother reports that during this time , her daughter has missed 2 days of school during each menstrual period because of severe pelvic cramps associated with vomiting . Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last 4 to 5 days. Her last menstrual period was 7 days ago . She currently takes acetaminophen , which provides minimal relief of her symptoms . She has had three lifetime sexual partners , and they use condoms inconsistently . The patient is an honor roll student despite frequent absences from school. Physical examination shows no abnormalities . Pelvic examination shows a tender, normal-sized uterus and no masses . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Primary dysmenorrhea, or painful menstruation, is a common cause of cyclic pelvic pain in healthy females and occurs in the absence of secondary causes, such as endometriosis, adenomyosis, cervical stenosis, or uterine fibroids. Symptoms often begin during adolescence and commonly interfere with quality of life and with essential activities such as school or work. Patients describe crampy lower abdominal or pelvic pain that begins several days prior to the onset of menses, which persists for several days, along with fatigue, nausea, vomiting, pre-syncopal symptoms, and headache. Endometrial sloughing is accompanied by the production of prostaglandins, which stimulate painful uterine contractions. Patients are typically treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs that inhibit cyclooxygenase enzymes, thereby limiting prostaglandin synthesis, or with oral hormonal contraceptives.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. A pregnancy test (Choice A) can be used to evaluate for pregnancy, particularly ectopic pregnancy in the setting of severe abdominal pain. However, this patient's most recent period was 7 days ago, making pregnancy unlikely. Pelvic ultrasonography (Choice B) can be used to evaluate for structural abnormalities of the uterus or adnexa, such as fibroids or ovarian cysts that can cause recurrent abdominopelvic pain. However, there was no evidence of structural abnormalities during this patient's pelvic examination. Narcotic therapy (Choice C) carries a high risk for physical dependence and opioid use disorder. It would be inappropriate to start narcotic therapy for pain control in this patient before trying other options, such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug therapy. Selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitor therapy (Choice E) is used in the treatment of major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder. It does not play a role in the management of primary dysmenorrhea. Educational Objective: Primary dysmenorrhea, or painful menstruation, is a common cause of cyclic pelvic pain in healthy females and occurs in the absence of secondary causes. Symptoms include crampy lower abdominal or pelvic pain that begins several days prior to the onset of menses and persists for several days, as well as fatigue, nausea, vomiting, pre-syncopal symptoms, and headache. Treatment includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 9-month-old boy is brought to the physician 2 months after his parents noticed that he seemed to be ignoring them. On questioning , they note that he does not appear to be startled by loud noises. Growth and development have been otherwise normal. He was born at term to a 28-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 1. His mother's blood group is A, Rh-negative , and his blood group is A, Rh-positive . He had a serum total bilirubin concentration of 25 mg/dL at the age of 2 days and received phototherapy for 2 days. He continued to be mildly jaundiced until the age of 1 month. Serum studies since then have shown no abnormalities . Examination today shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is most likely to have prevented this patient's current condition?
correctExplanation: Kernicterus occurs as a result of the deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in a newborn's brain, usually in the basal ganglia, pons, and cerebellum. It typically presents with poor feeding, lethargy, and seizures. If untreated, it can cause long-term neurologic abnormalities, such as gaze palsies or sensorineural hearing loss. Unconjugated or indirect bilirubin is circulating insoluble bilirubin that is largely bound to albumin. It has not yet undergone conjugation in the liver. Causes of increased unconjugated bilirubin include hemolysis, breast milk jaundice, Crigler-Najjar syndrome, Gilbert syndrome, and physiologic jaundice. In newborns, causes also include maternal exposure to sulfonamide antibiotics, which displace bilirubin from albumin in the neonate, thereby increasing the free plasma concentrations of unconjugated bilirubin. Kernicterus typically occurs when the bilirubin concentration exceeds 25-30 mg/dL, which is commonly caused by glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency or Rh-hemolytic disease of the newborn, the latter of which was likely present in this patient given the discordant Rh status of him and his mother. Risk factors include prematurity, cephalohematoma or significant bruising, poor breastfeeding, and East Asian ethnicity. Treatment to prevent severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and subsequent kernicterus is phototherapy or exchange transfusion. Exchange transfusions are particularly useful in hyperbilirubinemia that is caused by anti-Rh(D) antibodies, as they allow removal of the antibodies as well as the bilirubin.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Avoidance of breast-feeding (Choice A) could be considered in breast milk jaundice or breastfeeding jaundice, although it is usually not required as the increased bilirubin concentrations seen are typically benign. Breast milk jaundice is hypothesized to occur because of the presence of beta-glucuronidase in breast milk, which deconjugates bilirubin and allows it to be reabsorbed. Breastfeeding jaundice occurs as a result of relative hypovolemia secondary to inadequate intake, which results in hyperbilirubinemia. Water supplementation (Choice B) is generally not advised in infants, as their kidneys are incapable of properly reabsorbing sodium, which results in hyponatremia. This can cause altered mental status and seizures. Water supplementation is not used to treat hyperbilirubinemia. Longer course of phototherapy (Choice C) could have decreased the overall amount of unconjugated bilirubin, as phototherapy converts indirect bilirubin into a water-soluble form that can be excreted. However, it would have been less effective in this patient with severe hyperbilirubinemia likely secondary to anti-Rh(D) antibody-mediated hemolysis. Antibiotic therapy (Choice D) is used in the treatment of neonatal infections, such as Escherichia coli or Streptococcus aga/actiae meningitis. Bacterial meningitis is associated with a high mortality if untreated, as well as prolonged neurologic complications, such as hearing loss, even when treated. A missed diagnosis of bacterial meningitis would have certainly led to neonatal demise or significant morbidity. Educational Objective: Kernicterus is caused by high concentrations of unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, commonly in hemolysis because of Rh alloimmunization or glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. It is associated with poor feeding, lethargy, and seizures as a result of deposition of bilirubin in the basal ganglia, pons, and cerebellum. If untreated, it can lead to long-term neurologic sequelae, such as hearing loss. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 4-year-old boy has had fatigue , decreased appetite , and a 2.3-kg (5-lb) weight loss over the past 2 months. He appears listless . His pulse is 80/min while supine and 105/min while standing , and his blood pressure is 85/60 mm Hg while supine and 75/45 mm Hg while standing . Serum glucose concentration is 465 mg/dl . Urinalysis shows 3+ ketones , 4+ glucose , and 1 to 2 WBC/hpf . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: A pediatric patient presenting with fatigue, decreased appetite, weight loss, and hyperglycemia raises suspicion for type 1 diabetes mellitus. Type 1 diabetes mellitus can also be complicated by diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and patients can present with DKA as their initial manifestation. DKA can also result from increased insulin requirements during times of physiologic stress (eg, infection) or insulin nonadherence. DKA occurs as a result of the accumulation of serum ketones such as beta-hydroxybutyric acid, acetoacetic acid, and acetone in the setting of deficient insulin signaling. Dysregulated fatty acid degradation and ketone synthesis occurs because of the relative state of starvation created through absent insulin signaling. Type 1 diabetes mellitus can also result in dehydration caused by hyperglycemia, glucosuria, and osmotic diuresis. This diuresis can result in dehydration, ketonuria, and orthostasis. Orthostatic vital signs are significant pulse increases greater than 20/min, systolic pressure decreases over 20 mm Hg, or diastolic pressure decreases over 10 mm Hg with changes in position from supine to seated to standing. Because of the patient's osmotic diuresis, orthostatic hypotension, and dehydration, the first step in care requires the administration of 0.9% saline intravenously for fluid resuscitation.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Urine culture {Choice A) would not be the next appropriate step for this patient. Urinary tract infection is unlikely in a patient without symptoms of dysuria, urinary urgency, or frequency, and less than 5-10 WBC/hpf on urinalysis. Urinalysis discloses ketones and glucose, consistent with DKA, and the patient would benefit from fluid resuscitation. Oral glucose tolerance test {Choice B) is typically performed to evaluate for type 2 diabetes mellitus or for maternal gestational diabetes between 24 and 28 weeks' gestation. Gestational diabetes can lead to an increased risk for congenital anomalies, spontaneous abortion and stillbirth, macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, and birth trauma. In a patient with a random glucose greater than 200 mg/dl and associated symptoms, the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus can be made. Measurement of hemoglobin A 1c {Choice C) is useful for the diagnosis and long-term management of diabetes mellitus. It would be less helpful in the acute management of a new diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and DKA. Administration of subcutaneous insulin {Choice D) can be helpful in this patient, although insulin should be administered intravenously for the management of DKA once the patient is appropriately resuscitated with intravenous fluid. In a patient with signs of dehydration and orthostasis, intravenous fluid resuscitation should be the first step in management. Educational Objective: Type 1 diabetes mellitus and diabetic ketoacidosis can result in significant dehydration caused by hyperglycemia, glucosuria, and osmotic diuresis. The first step in care requires fluid resuscitation with intravenous isotonic fluids. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous
